extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying discrete mathematics/introductory proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and solution patterns for proving relations are equivalence relations, describing their equivalence classes, and proving properties of functions (injective, surjective, bijective), plus standard set/image/preimage identities and counting arguments used in discrete math exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that a binary relation R is an equivalence relation one must show it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical proofs check each property in turn. Examples in the text: show 3 | (x^2 − x^2) for reflexivity; if 3 | (x^2 − y^2) then 3 | (y^2 − x^2) for symmetry; for transitivity write x^2 − z^2 = (x^2 − y^2) + (y^2 − z^2) and use integer sums. For slope-based relations check vertical/slope cases for each property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine equivalence classes by characterizing the invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: An element (or representative) belongs to an equivalence class [(a)] iff it shares the invariant used by the relation (e.g., same sum x^2+y^2, same slope, same residue class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe classes geometrically/algebraically: e.g., for (x,y) ~ (a,b) iff x^2+y^2 = a^2+b^2 the class [(a,b)] is the circle of radius sqrt(a^2+b^2) (with (0,0) special case). For line-slope relation classes are sets of lines with the same slope (include vertical line as slope ∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify congruence/divisibility relations using residues (Division Algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find equivalence classes for relations defined via congruences or divisibility, reduce integers to their residues modulo n and compute the relevant transformed residues (e.g., squares mod n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: to classify x such that 3 | x^2−y^2 compute squares of residues {0,1,2} mod 3; for 7a^2 ≡ 2b^2 (mod 5) write a=5q_a+r_a, b=5q_b+r_b and compare 2 r_a^2 (mod 5) values to partition classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove transitivity for divisibility-based relations by adding representations
rubrics_metrics.description: When relations are defined by divisibility (e.g., n | expression), prove transitivity by expressing the relevant differences as integer multiples and adding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: if x^2−y^2 = 3k and y^2−z^2 = 3ℓ then x^2−z^2 = 3(k+ℓ), concluding 3 | (x^2−z^2). Use k, ℓ ∈ Z and closure under addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a family is a partition: union covers and parts pairwise disjoint
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a collection R of subsets is a partition of A prove (1) union of elements of R equals A, and (2) distinct members of R are disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove union coverage by taking arbitrary x∈A and producing S∈P and T∈Q s.t. x∈S∩T∈R; prove pairwise disjointness by contrapositive: if U1∩U2 ≠ ∅ then show U1 = U2 via uniqueness properties of the underlying partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a relation on power set defined via a distinguished element is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: When relations on 𝒫(E) are defined via membership of a fixed q (e.g., A ℛ B iff (q∈A)∨(q∈B) type expressions), prove reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity by case analysis on membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logic of intersections/unions and examine exhaustive cases (as in the four-case analysis in the text) to establish transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: To establish a mapping is a function: uniqueness of y for every x
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that for each x in domain there exists exactly one y in codomain satisfying the defining condition (so that the relation defines a well-defined function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for relation defined by ax + by = 6 solve for y = (6 − a x)/b and require this to be integer for all x∈Z; testing x=0 and x=1 yields divisibility constraints b|6 and b|a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove image/preimage set identity by element-chasing both inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show equalities like f^{-1}(E − F) = f^{-1}(E) − f^{-1}(F), prove both ⊆ and ⊇ by taking arbitrary elements and following definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the standard pattern: start with x ∈ f^{-1}(E − F) ⇒ f(x) ∈ E − F ⇒ f(x) ∈ E and f(x) ∉ F ⇒ x ∈ f^{-1}(E) and x ∉ f^{-1}(F), etc. Use modus tollens where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of a set difference under injective f equals difference of images; injectivity necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: For any function f, f(A) − f(B) ⊆ f(A − B) always holds; equality f(A − B) = f(A) − f(B) holds when f is injective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: inclusion f(A − B) ⊆ f(A) − f(B) uses injectivity to rule out preimages in B; the contrapositive argument shows failure of inclusion implies non-injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove injectivity: show f(x)=f(y) implies x=y (element chase or structural reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish injectivity by assuming equality of outputs and deducing equality of inputs, often exploiting parity, uniqueness of factorization, or algebraic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: parity argument (2n+1 odd forces exponent of 2 zero) and unique prime factorization are used to show injectivity for pairing functions; simple algebraic cancellation works for linear functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove surjectivity: for each y construct an x with f(x)=y (constructive inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate surjectivity by giving an explicit formula or construction producing a preimage x for an arbitrary y in the codomain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: invert quadratics by completing the square and taking square roots; for f : [3,∞)→[5,∞) set x = 3 + sqrt(y−5). For discrete maps use prime factorization to decompose n and recover (a,b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove bijection by proving both injective and surjective (and/or constructing inverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show both injectivity and surjectivity, or explicitly give the inverse mapping, to establish a bijection between sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: construct g : 𝒫(A)→𝒫(B) from a bijection f:A→B by g(X)={f(x):x∈X} and verify injectivity/surjectivity; for N×N↔N use formula 2^{a−1}(2b−1) and invert by prime factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count functions A→{0,1} and relate to power set via indicator mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 2^{|A|} functions from a finite set A to {0,1}; map each function to the subset of A mapped to 1 to obtain a bijection with 𝒫(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: each element has two choices yielding 2^n functions; define g(f) = {a ∈ A : f(a) = 1} and prove g is injective and surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prime factorization/2-adic valuation to build/invert pairing functions
rubrics_metrics.description: When coding pairs into integers, separate powers of 2 (even/odd parts) to recover components uniquely using unique factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: n = 2^{a−1}(2b−1) is surjective because the odd part equals 2ℓ−1 for some ℓ; injectivity follows because differing exponents of 2 would change parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove binomial coefficient divisibility by a prime p for 0
rubrics_metrics.description: Show p divides p! in numerator but none of the denominator factors (which are < p), hence p | (p choose k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that numerator contains factor p and denominator is product of integers < p so cannot cancel p. Conclude that binomial coefficients (p choose k) are multiples of p for 0<k<p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pascal's identity and induction to prove integrality of binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Pascal's recursion and induction on n to show every binomial coefficient is an integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case n=0 trivial; for k between boundaries apply n choose r = (n−1 choose r−1) + (n−1 choose r) and use inductive hypothesis that the summands are integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe ranges of vector-valued functions by eliminating parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the range of a function θ: R^2 → R^3 given by (5y,4x,x+y), eliminate x,y to get an equation (linear relation) that coordinates must satisfy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve for x,y in terms of coordinates (a,b,c) and obtain relation c = a/5 + b/4, so the range is the plane 20z − 4a − 5b = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameterize equivalence classes by a parameter space (e.g., slopes, radii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalence classes can often be indexed by a parameter: for slope relation use m∈R∪{∞}; for x^2+y^2 invariance use r>0 (radius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick canonical representatives (line through origin with slope m, vertical ℓ_∞, (0,r) or (r,0)) and list classes as {[ℓ_m]: m∈R}∪{[ℓ_∞]} or {[(0,r)]: r>0} together with [(0,0)].

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify units and orbits in Z_n via multiplicative invertibles
rubrics_metrics.description: When relation is defined by multiplication by a unit in Z_n, compute the set U of invertible residues and form orbits [x]_n = {x·u : u∈U}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Z6 units U = {[1]_6,[5]_6} so classes like [[1]_6] = {[1]_6,[5]_6}, [[2]_6] = {[2]_6,[4]_6}, etc. Use multiplication tables to identify units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Bézout's identity to combine divisibility conditions and deduce gcd/lcm properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Bézout (existence of x,y with ax+by=gcd(a,b)) to derive divisibility conclusions like: if 3|n and 8|n and gcd(3,8)=1 then 24|n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply Bézout equation by n and use given divisibilities to show n is multiple of lcm; use explicit x,y from Bézout as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove modular congruence properties of primes by splitting into small modulus checks
rubrics_metrics.description: To show statements like p^2 ≡ 1 (mod 24) for prime p≥5, show separately that 3 | (p^2−1) and 8 | (p^2−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modulus 3 use p≡1 or 2 (mod3) gives p^2≡1. For modulus 8 use parity representation p=2k+1 and analyze k even/odd to show 8 divides p^2−1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equality by showing mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard technique: to show X=Y prove X⊆Y and Y⊆X separately, often used for image, union or partition equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly in proofs: e.g., f(R)=[−1,1] done by proving f(R)⊆[−1,1] via inequalities and [−1,1]⊆f(R) by explicit inverse construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a function is not injective or not surjective via counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove injectivity find two distinct inputs with same output; to disprove surjectivity find a codomain element with no preimage (often by a bound on range).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show f is not injective by finding x1≠x2 with f(x1)=f(x2) (complete square yields two roots); show not surjective by showing f(x)≥m for all x and pick y<m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong induction to prove uniqueness properties of functions on N under order constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:N→N is injective and f(n)≤n, strong induction can show f(n)=n for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base: f(1)≤1 and f(1)∈N ⇒ f(1)=1. Inductive step: assume f(k)=k for k≤n, then f(n+1)∈{1,...,n+1} cannot equal any k≤n by injectivity, so f(n+1)=n+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: When defining a function on equivalence classes, check well-definedness
rubrics_metrics.description: A function on classes f: S→T given by f([(x)]) = φ(x) must be checked: if [(x)] = [(y)] then φ(x)=φ(y), so f is well-defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define f([(x,y)]) = sqrt(x^2+y^2). Show that if (x,y)~(s,t) (same x^2+y^2) then the assigned value is identical, hence f is a valid function on the set of classes.
